title: Register and idiom
summary: After this unit you can match register to each paper, use idioms naturally in Speaking and avoid them in Writing, and choose between phrasal and single-word verbs.

items.title: Register is part of Lexical Resource
body: The band 9 descriptors refer to vocabulary used with 'very natural and sophisticated control', and at band 7 and above the examiner checks 'awareness of style'. In practice this means matching register to the task: Writing Task 1 and 2 are **formal-neutral academic**; Speaking is **neutral-informal conversation**.
Both directions cost marks. Slang and contractions in an essay sound careless; essay language in Speaking (*Furthermore, it is my contention that...*) sounds memorised and unnatural.
list: **Neutral**: *The government doesn't want to get involved.* (Speaking, or neutral writing without the contraction)
**Informal**: *The government's staying well out of it.* (relaxed speech only)

items.title: Features of academic register in Writing
body: Academic writing is impersonal and precise, but not pompous.
list: Few personal pronouns, except to state your position (*I believe*); avoid addressing the reader as *you*.
Precise quantifiers instead of vague ones: *a significant minority* rather than *loads of people*.
No rhetorical questions or exclamation marks.
Neutral or formal single-word verbs where they are more precise: *investigate* rather than *look into*, though common phrasal verbs are acceptable (see lesson 3).

examples.text: Loads of people can't afford to buy a house these days, which is pretty awful.
examples.note: Informal: loads of, can't, these days, pretty awful.

examples.text: A growing number of people are unable to afford to buy a home, which is a cause for serious concern.

items.title: Features of natural spoken register
body: In Speaking, natural register includes contractions, discourse markers (*well*, *actually*, *I mean*), vague language used appropriately (*sort of*, *and so on*, *a bit*), and personal examples. These are signs of fluency, not of informality to be avoided.
Keep it neutral rather than slangy. *It was a bit of a nightmare* is perfect; *It was well dodgy, innit* is not appropriate in an exam.

options: A  Formal academic (suitable for Task 2)
B  Neutral spoken (suitable for Speaking)
C  Too informal for the exam

rows.label: It is widely acknowledged that urban green space benefits mental health.
I think parks make a big difference, actually, especially if you live in a flat.
Parks are dead good for your head, no joke.
A significant proportion of respondents expressed dissatisfaction with the service.
Honestly, most people I know aren't that bothered about it.

items.why: Formal academic sentences are impersonal and precise; neutral spoken ones use contractions and markers like *actually* and *honestly*; slang (*dead good*, *no joke*) is inappropriate in both papers.

items.q: Which sentence is most appropriate in a Task 2 essay?
options: Kids these days spend loads of time on their phones.
Children now spend a considerable amount of time on their phones.
Kiddos are always glued to their screens, aren't they?
You know how children are always on their phones.
items.why: B is formal-neutral and precise. A and C use informal vocabulary, C has a rhetorical tag question, and D addresses the reader as *you*.

items.q: Which answer sounds most natural in Speaking Part 1? Q: 'Do you like your neighbourhood?'
options: It is my firm conviction that my neighbourhood possesses numerous advantages.
Yeah, I do, actually. It's quiet, but there are a couple of good cafés within walking distance.
Affirmative. The neighbourhood is satisfactory.
Furthermore, my neighbourhood is good. Moreover, it is quiet.
items.why: B uses natural spoken features (*Yeah*, *actually*, contractions) and a concrete detail. The others are inappropriately formal or mechanical.

items.text: Rewrite formally: 'lots of young people' becomes 'a ___ number of young people'.
items.why: *A large / considerable / significant number of* is the formal equivalent.
*Children* is the neutral-formal word; *kids* is informal.

items.text: Rewrite formally: 'It's a really big deal' becomes 'It is a matter of considerable ___'.
items.why: *Of considerable importance* is formal and precise.

items.q: Which feature is a mistake in Task 2?
options: Using *I believe* in the introduction to state your position.
Writing *don't* and *isn't*.
Using the passive to report others' views.
Using precise quantifiers like *a minority*.
items.why: Contractions are inappropriate in academic writing. Stating your own view with *I believe* is perfectly acceptable in Task 2.

items.title: Idioms in Speaking: natural, not decorative
body: The band descriptors for Lexical Resource in Speaking mention 'idiomatic language' from band 7 upwards. What examiners reward is idiomatic *usage*: natural phrasal verbs, collocations and fixed expressions used in the right place (*it's not my cup of tea*, *I'm in two minds*, *it takes a while to get used to*).

What they do not reward is a memorised idiom pushed into an answer where it does not fit. *It was raining cats and dogs* or *It was a piece of cake* are widely taught, rarely used by native speakers, and examiners hear them dozens of times a day.
list: Natural in Speaking: *I'm in two minds about it*, *it's not really my thing*, *I've got a lot on at the moment*, *it was a bit of an eye-opener*, *it costs an arm and a leg* (used sparingly), *off the top of my head*
Overused and dated: *raining cats and dogs*, *a piece of cake*, *once in a blue moon* (in every answer), *as fit as a fiddle*, *over the moon*
items.tip: Use an idiom only if you would genuinely say it to a friend in English, and only if it fits the meaning exactly.

items.title: Idioms in Writing: mostly avoid
body: In Task 2, idioms usually lower the register and often sound like clichés. *A double-edged sword*, *the tip of the iceberg*, *a hot potato* and *at the end of the day* are best replaced by precise literal language.

Some fixed expressions are fully acceptable in academic writing because they are neutral: *in the long run*, *on the whole*, *by and large*, *a vicious circle*, *come at a cost*, *the root cause*. These are collocations rather than colourful idioms.

examples.text: Social media is a double-edged sword.
Social media brings clear benefits but also carries significant risks.
Poverty and poor health can form a vicious circle.
examples.note: A neutral fixed expression, perfectly acceptable in Writing.

items.q: Where would each expression be appropriate?
options: A  Natural in Speaking
B  Acceptable in both Speaking and Writing
C  Best avoided (cliché or overused)

rows.label: I'm in two minds about it.
It was raining cats and dogs.
Every cloud has a silver lining.
off the top of my head

items.why: Conversational idioms suit Speaking; neutral fixed expressions work anywhere; proverbs and textbook idioms sound memorised in both papers.

items.q: Which Part 1 answer uses idiomatic language most naturally? Q: 'Do you enjoy cooking?'
options: Cooking is a piece of cake and I am over the moon when I do it.
Not really, to be honest. It's not my thing. I can throw something together, but I'd rather someone else did it.
Once in a blue moon I cook, and it costs an arm and a leg, and it's raining cats and dogs.
I enjoy cooking very much because it is enjoyable.
items.why: B uses natural, current expressions (*not my thing*, *throw something together*) that fit the meaning exactly. A and C pile up textbook idioms; D has no idiomatic language at all.

items.q: Which is the best replacement in a Task 2 essay for 'Pollution is just the tip of the iceberg'?
options: Pollution is only the most visible part of a much larger problem.
Pollution is the cherry on the cake.
Pollution is a whole other kettle of fish.
Pollution is no walk in the park.
items.why: A says the same thing in precise, neutral language suited to academic writing. The other options swap one idiom for another, often with the wrong meaning.

items.text: Q: 'Would you like to live abroad?' A: 'I'm in two ___ about it, really. I'd love the experience, but I'd miss my family.'
items.why: *In two minds* means undecided, a natural spoken idiom.

items.text: Part 2: 'Moving to London was a real eye-___. I hadn't realised how expensive everything would be.'
items.why: *An eye-opener* is something that reveals surprising information.

items.text: Task 2: 'Low wages and poor housing can trap families in a vicious ___.'
items.why: *A vicious circle / cycle* is a neutral fixed expression acceptable in academic writing.

items.q: Which sentence uses an idiom with the wrong meaning?
options: Learning to drive took a while, but once I got the hang of it, I loved it.
My exam was a real eye-opener, so I passed it easily.
I've got a lot on at the moment, so I haven't been to the gym.
Off the top of my head, I'd say about twenty people came.
items.why: *An eye-opener* means a surprising revelation, not something easy. The other idioms are used accurately.

items.title: Two vocabularies for the same meaning
body: English often has a phrasal verb of Germanic origin and a single-word verb of Latin or French origin for similar meanings: *find out / discover*, *set up / establish*, *cut down on / reduce*, *put off / postpone*, *bring about / cause*.

Phrasal verbs are not informal by nature, but many are more conversational. In Speaking, phrasal verbs sound natural and fluent; replacing them all with Latinate verbs makes you sound stiff. In Writing, many neutral phrasal verbs are perfectly acceptable (*carry out research*, *set up a business*), but very colloquial ones (*mess up*, *get by*) should be replaced.

items.title: Choosing well
body: In Task 2, prefer the single-word verb when it is more precise or when the phrasal verb is informal (*mess up*, *get round*). Keep the phrasal verb when it is the normal neutral term (*carry out*, *set up*, *phase out*) or when the Latinate alternative would sound pompous.

In Speaking, do the opposite: phrasal verbs show natural control. *We put the meeting off till Friday* sounds natural; *We postponed the meeting until Friday* sounds like a written announcement, though neither is wrong.

examples.text: Governments should get rid of fossil fuel subsidies.
Governments should phase out fossil fuel subsidies.
Governments should eliminate fossil fuel subsidies.

items.q: Choose the best verb for a Task 2 essay.
options: A  investigate
B  establish
C  reduce
D  postpone
E  eliminate

rows.label: Governments should ___ (cut down on) their reliance on imported energy.
It is far easier to ___ (set up) a small business online than it once was.
The council plans to ___ (look into) the causes of the flooding.
The decision was ___ (put off) until more data was available.
New technology could ___ (get rid of) the need for manual checks entirely.

items.why: Each single-word verb is more formal and precise than the phrasal verb in brackets. Note *was postponed* for the passive.

items.q: Which sentence sounds most natural in Speaking Part 1?
options: I endeavoured to ascertain the time of the film.
I tried to find out what time the film started.
I attempted to discover the commencement time of the film.
I sought to determine the film's start.
items.why: B uses a natural phrasal verb (*find out*) and everyday words. The others are absurdly formal for casual speech.

items.q: Which phrasal verb is acceptable in a formal essay?
options: Scientists carried out a series of experiments.
The government totally messed up the reform.
Families can barely get by on one salary.
Politicians often try to wriggle out of their promises.
items.why: *Carry out* is the standard neutral verb with *experiments*, *research* and *surveys*. The others are colloquial.

items.text: Speaking: 'I've been meaning to take ___ a new hobby, maybe climbing.'
items.why: *Take up* a hobby means start it: natural and neutral.

items.text: Writing: 'Many countries plan to ___ out petrol cars by 2035.'
items.why: *Phase out* means gradually stop using, a neutral phrasal verb common in formal writing.

items.text: Writing: 'Wages have failed to keep ___ with inflation.'
items.why: *Keep pace with* (more formal) or *keep up with* (neutral).

items.text: Writing: 'The committee will ___ the matter before making a recommendation.' (= look into)
items.why: *Investigate* or *examine* is the formal single-word equivalent of *look into*.

items: To be honest, I keep putting it off,
but I really need to sort out
all the stuff in my garage
items.why: Phrasal verbs (*put off*, *sort out*) and *stuff* are natural in Speaking, where they signal relaxed fluency.
